'''yern<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' An old form of ''iron.''

'''yerne†''', ''adv.'' [ME., < AS. ''georne'', eagerly, < ''georn'', eager: see ''yarn''<sup>1</sup>, ''yern''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''] '''1.''' Soon; early.
{{smaller block|<poem>If I late or ''yerne''
Wold it biwreye, or dorst, or sholde, or konne.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 376.}}}}
'''2.''' Quickly; promptly.
{{smaller block|<poem>What nede were it this preyere for to werne,
Syne ye shul both han folk and toun as ''yerne''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 112.}}}}

'''yerney†''', ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''irony''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|Thou didste beholde it vntil there came a stone smyten out without handis, which smitte the image vpon his ''yerney'' & erthen feete, breking them al to powlder.
{{right|''Joye'', Expos. of Daniel, ii.}}}}

'''yernful†''', ''a.'' A spelling of ''yearnful.''

'''yernut, yarnut''' (yėr′nut, yär′nut), ''n.'' [See ''arnot'', ''earthnut.''] The earthnut or hawknut, ''Conopodium denudatum'' (''Bunium flexuosum'').

'''yes''' (yes), ''adv.'' [Also dial. ''yis''; < ME. ''ȝis'', ''ȝus'', < AS. ''gise'', ''gese'', yes; perhaps reduced, by reason of its frequent use and its essentially unitary meaning, from ''geá sī'', ‘yea, be it (so)’: ''geá'', yea; ''sī'', ''sȳ'' (= G. ''sei'' = L. ''sit'', etc.), 3d pers. pl. subj. of ''beón'', be: see ''be''<sup>1</sup>. It is possible that the second element is a reduced form of ''swā'', so; cf. F. Sp. Pg. It. ''si'', yes, < L. ''sic'', so.] A word which expresses affirmation or consent: opposed to ''no.'' It is also used, like ''yea'', to enforce by repetition or addition something which precedes.

{{smaller block|<poem>''Hast.'' But, by your leave, it never yet did hurt
To lay down likelihoods and forms of hope.
''L. Bard.'' ''Yes,'' if this present quality of war,
Indeed the instant action: a cause on foot
Lives so in hope as in an early spring
We see the appearing buds.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 3. 36.}}
''Yes,'' you despise the man to books confin’d.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, i. 1.}}
<poem>''May.'' See, see! what ’s he walks yonder? is he mad?
''Full.'' That ’s a musician: ''yes,'' he ’s besides himself.</poem>
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iv. 4.}}
<poem>Will spring return? . . .
''Yes,'' prattlers, ''yes.'' The daisy’s flower
Again shall paint your summer bower.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, i., Int.}}}}

{{smaller|[For distinction between ''yes'' and ''yea, no'' and ''nay,'' see ''yea.'']}}

''gestern,'' adv. yesterday (OHG. ''ē-gestern,'' day after to-morrow, day before yesterday), = Goth. ''gistra'' (in ''gistradagis,'' to-morrow) = L. ''hesternus,'' of yesterday; with orig. compar. suffix ''-tra,'' from a base (Teut. ''yes-'') seen in Icel. ''gær, gör'' = Dan. ''gaar'' (in

Remaining too, whom ''yester'' sun beheld

'''yesterday''' (yes′tėr-dạ̄), ''adv.'' [Also dial. ''yisterday''; < ME. ''yesterday'', ''ȝisterdai'', ''ȝusterdai'', ''ȝhistredai'', ''ȝurstendai'', < AS. ''geostrandæg'', ''giestrandæg'', ''gystrandæg'' = D. ''gisteren dag'', ''dag van gister'', yesterday, = Goth. ''gistradagis'' (found only once, in the alternative sense ‘to-morrow’); = L. ''hesterno die'', yesterday; as ''yester-'' + ''day''<sup>1</sup>.] On the day preceding this day; on the day last past.
{{smaller block|Thei seiden to hym, For [Fro] ''ȝistirdai'' in the seuenthe our the feuer lefte him. {{right|''Wyclif'', John iv. 52.}}
<poem>I saw him ''yesterday'', or t’ other day.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 1. 56.}}}}

'''yesterday''' (yes′tėr-dạ̄), ''n.'' [< ''yesterday'', ''adv.''] The day last past; the day next before the present: often used figuratively for time not long gone by; time in the immediate past.
{{smaller block|We are but of ''yesterday'', and know nothing. Job viii. 9.
<poem>To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow,
Creeps in this petty pace from day to day
To the last syllable of recorded time,</poem>}}
readings.c2s2:
<poem>And all our ''yesterdays'' have lighted fools
The way to dusty death. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 5. 22.</poem>

{{smaller block|I love to watch how the day, tired as it is, lags away reluctantly, and hates to be called ''yesterday'' so soon.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xiv.}}}}

'''yestereve''' (yes′tėr-ēv), ''adv.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''ȝisterneve''; a later form of ''yestereven''.] Same as ''yestereven''.
{{smaller block|<poem>In hope that you would come here
''Yester-eve.''</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', The Satyr.}}}}

'''yestereven''' (yes′tėr-ē″vn), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''yistereven'', ''ȝusturevyn''; < ''yester-'' + ''even''<sup>2</sup>.] On the evening of the day preceding the present.

'''yestereven''' (yes′tėr-ē″vn), ''n.'' [< ''yestereven'', ''adv.''] The evening last past.
{{smaller block|<poem>And dim grows Atli’s roof-sun
O’er ''yestereven’s'' feast.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Sigurd, iv.}}}}

'''yesterevening''' (yes′tėr-ēv″ning), ''n.'' [< ''yester-'' + ''evening''.] Same as ''yestereven''.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Village . . . had been seized and fired
Late on the ''yester-evening''.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Destiny of Nations.}}}}

'''yesterfang†''' (yes′tėr-fang), ''n.'' [< ''yester-'' + ''fang''.] That which was taken, captured, or caught on the previous day or former occasion.
{{smaller block|Although milians and infinite numbers of them [fish] be taken, yet on the next [day] their losse will be so supplied with new store that nothing shall be missing of the ''yesterfang''.
{{right|''Boethius'', Descrip. of Scotland (trans.), ix. (Holinshed’s [Chron., I.).}}}}

'''yestermorn''' (yes′tėr-môrn), ''n.'' [< ''yester-'' + ''morn.''] The morn or morning before the present; the morning last past. ''Rowe.''
{{smaller block|<poem>And a dozen-segars are lingering yet
Of the thousand of ''yestermorn.''</poem>
{{right|''Halleck'', Epistles, etc.}}}}

'''yestermorning''' (yes′tėr-môr″ning), ''n.'' [< ''yester-'' + ''morning.''] Same as ''yestermorn.''

'''yesternight''' (yes′tėr-nīt), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''ȝesterniȝt, ȝisterniȝt, ȝusterniȝt, yerstenenight''; < ''yester-'' + ''night.''] On the night last past.
{{smaller block|My lord, I think I saw him ''yesternight.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2. 189.}}}}
{{smaller block|I was invited ''yesternight'' to a solemn Supper.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 13.}}}}

'''yesternight''' (yes′tėr-nīt), ''n.'' [< ''yesternight'', ''adv.''] The night last past.
{{smaller block|<poem>I saw their boats, with many a light,
Floating the livelong ''yesternight.''</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iv. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Come not as thou camest of late,
Flinging the gloom of ''yesternight''
On the white day. ''Tennyson'', Ode to Memory.</poem>}}

'''yester-year''' (yes′tėr-yēr), ''n.'' Last year. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|But where are the snows of ''yester-year?''
{{right|''D. G. Rossetti'', Ballad of Dead Ladies.}}}}

'''yestreen''' (yes-trēn′), ''adv.'' [Contracted from ''yestereven.''] Last evening; last night; yesternight. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The bridegroom may forget the bride,
Was made his wedded wife ''yestreen.''</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Lament for Glencairn.}}}}

'''yesty†''', ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''yeasty.''
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''yet'''<sup>1</sup> (yet), ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [Also dial. ''yit''; < ME. ''yet'', ''ʒet'', ''ʒit'', < AS. ''git'', ''get'', ''giet'', ''gyt'', ''gita'', ''geta'' = OFries. ''ieta'', ''eta'', ''ita'', Fries. ''jiette'' = MHG. ''iezuo'', ''ieze'', G. ''ietz'', now ''jetzt'', archaic ''jetzo''; also MHG. ''iezunt'', G. ''jetzund'', now; origin uncertain; the MHG. ''iezuo'' is appar. < ''ie'', ever (or a form cognate with AS. ''ge'', and), + ''zuo'', to; but it may merely simulate ''zuo''. For a similar case in which an orig. significant terminal syllable or independent word has probably been reduced, see ''yes''.] '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' At or in the present time or juncture; before something else; at present; now: as, shall the deed be done ''yet''? is it time ''yet''?
{{smaller block|<poem>You have often
Begun to tell me what I am, but stopp’d, . . .
Concluding, “Stay: not ''yet''.”</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 37.}}
He [Thales] was reputed one of the wise men that made answer to the question when a man should marry — “A young man, not ''yet''; an elder man, not at all.”
{{right|''Bacon'', Marriage and Single Life (ed. 1887).}}}}
'''2.''' In addition; over and above; in repetition; further; besides; still; even: used especially with comparatives.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Yet'' more quarrelling with occasion!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 5. 60.}}
<poem>''Yet'' once more, O ye laurels, . . .
I come to pluck your berries harsh and crude.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' Still, in continuance of a former state; at this or at that time, as formerly; now or then, as at a previous period.
{{smaller block|And it [Jaffa] was oon of the fyrst Cityes of the world ffounde by Japheth, Noes sonne, and bereth ''yett'' hys name.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 24.}}}}

'''yet'''<sup>1</sup> (yet), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [Also dial. ''yit''; < ME. ''yet'', ''ʒet'', ''ʒit'', < AS. ''git'', ''get'', ''giet'', ''gyt'', ''gita'', ''geta'' = OFries. ''ieta'', ''eta'', ''ita'', Fries. ''jiette'' = MHG. ''iezuo'', ''ieze'', G. ''ietz'', now ''jetzt'', archaic ''jetzo''; also MHG. ''iezunt'', G. ''jetzund'', now; origin uncertain; the MHG. ''iezuo'' is appar. < ''ie'', ever (or a form cognate with AS. ''ge'', and), + ''zuo'', to; but it may merely simulate ''zuo''. For a similar case in which an orig. significant terminal syllable or independent word has probably been reduced, see ''yes''.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' At or in the present time or juncture; before something else; at present; now: as, shall the deed be done ''yet''? is it time ''yet''?
{{smaller block|<poem>You have often
Begun to tell me what I am, but stopp’d, . . .
Concluding, “Stay: not ''yet''.”</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|He [Thales] was reputed one of the wise men that made answer to the question when a man should marry — “A young man, not ''yet''; an elder man, not at all.”
{{right|''Bacon'', Marriage and Single Life (ed. 1887).}}}}
'''2.''' In addition; over and above; in repetition; further; besides; still; even: used especially with comparatives.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Yet'' more quarrelling with occasion!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 5. 60.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Yet'' once more, O ye laurels, . . .
I come to pluck your berries harsh and crude.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' Still, in continuance of a former state; at this or at that time, as formerly; now or then, as at a previous period.
{{smaller block|And it [Jaffa] was oon of the fyrst Cityes of the world ffounde by Japheth, Noes sonne, and bereth ''yett'' hys name.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 24.}}}}

{{smaller block|While we were ''yet'' sinners, Christ died for us. Rom. v. 8.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I see him ''yet'', the princely boy!</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., ii. 32.}}}}
'''4.''' At or before some future time; before all is done.
{{smaller block|Hope thou in God; for I shall ''yet'' praise him. Ps. xlii. 11.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He’ll be hanged ''yet'',
Though every drop of water
. . . gape . . . to glut him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 1. 61.}}}}
'''5.''' Up to the present time; thus far; hitherto; already: usually with a negative.
{{smaller block|The Holy Ghost was not ''yet'' given; because that Jesus was not ''yet'' glorified. John vii. 39.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let me remember thee what thou hast promised,
Which is not ''yet'' performed me.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 244.}}}}
{{smaller block|Opportunity hath baulked them ''yet''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Iland, not ''yet'' Britain but Albion, was in a manner desert and inhospitable.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., i.}}}}
''Yet'' is often accompanied by ''as'' in this sense: as, I have not met him ''as yet''.
{{smaller block|Unreconciled ''as yet'' to heaven.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 72.}}}}
'''6.''' Though the case be such; at least; at any rate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Madam, if your heart be so obdurate,
Vouchsafe me ''yet'' your picture for my love.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 2. 121.}}}}
{{smaller block|An unhappy François who, after passing eighteen years in prison, ''yet'' won the grace and love of Joan of Naples by his charms.
{{right|''J. A. Symonds'', Italy and Greece, p. 330.}}}}
''Yet'' is sometimes used with adjectives or participles (with or without a hyphen) to denote continuance of the action or state, or as equivalent to ''still''.

<poem>He rose, and saw the field deform’d with blood,
An empty space where late the coursers stood,
The ''yet''-warm Thracians panting on the coast.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, x. 612.}}}}
<poem>Lavaine
Returning brought the ''yet''-unblazon’d shield.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}

'''II.''' ''conj.'' '''1.''' Nevertheless; notwithstanding.
{{smaller block|He restored the chief butler unto his butlership again; . . . ''yet'' did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.
{{right|Gen. xl. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Blasted, and burnt, and blinded as I was, . . .
O, ''yet'' methought I saw the Holy Grail.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}
'''2.''' Though.
{{smaller block|I cannot speak to her, ''yet'' she urged conference.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2. 270.}}}}
'''3.''' But.
{{smaller block|<poem>“No, no,” quoth she, “sweet Death, I did but jest;
''Yet'', pardon me, I felt a kind of fear.”</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 998.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many perished raving mad, fancying themselves swimming in boundless seas, ''yet'' unable to assuage their thirst.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 45.}}}}

'''yet'''<sup>2</sup> (yet), ''v. t.''   [Sc. also ''yit''; < ME. ''yeten'', ''ʒeten'', < AS. ''geótan'', pour: see ''gush''.]   To melt; found; cast, as metal. [Obsolete or provincial.]
{{smaller block|To ''ʒett''; fundere, fusare.
{{right|''Cath. Ang.'', p. 426.}}}}
{{smaller block|''ʒetynge'' of metelle, as bellys, pannys, potys, and other lyke.
{{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 538.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
